r Editorial Why a Labor Paper? Because organized Labor represents 7,000 people in Tompkins and Cortland Counties. r Because Union members exist in every sector of our local economy, from industrial to professional; from mines to classrooms; from offices to hotels. Despite our importance, we are not considered “newsworthy” by the rest of the local media. Because Labor, not business, creates all wealth. Our many accomplishments deserve full recogni- tion. We're the backbone of the economy; we’re the people Paying our fair share of taxes; we're the peo- ind the United Way and who donate our ood. Because when the Ithaca Journal covers a Labor story all they see is the bad side. The Journal sees on- ly strikes and conflict when it sees Labor. The Jour- nal almost never covers the positive contributions that Labor makes to this community. <6 Because the Journal itself is a Union-buster, the winner of our Labor Coalition’s first “Goat of the Year’ award. The Journal has denied its own staff a contract over basic issues such as a wage scale and binding arbitration. * Because Labor, not business, creates all wealth. Our many accomplishments deserve full recognition. e’re the backbone of the economy; we’re the people Paying our fair share of taxes; we’re the people who the United Way and who donate our blood. Because the Ithaca Times, despite its (or perhaps because of its) liberal, upper middle class yearnings, still thinks that Unions are big, troubling bureaucracies; that Unions are not the same as the workers we represent. Because the Times understands social issues much better than it understands economic issues. Because the Grapevine has never seemed in- terested in covering the struggles and successes of working people. Because every day the Ithaca Journal devotes an entire page to Business interests and offered Labor only four columns per year on that page. Because working people simply do not hear about each struggles. Without better commiinica- tion among Unions and between working people, we can never unite to change out community for the better. Because our time has come — IF we understand that we, as workers, have fundamentally common interests; jobs, secure jobs, decent housing, education for our children, time for leisure, and the chance to grow and better ourselves and our world. Coming to Ithaca Soon AI Plant Closing Legislation by Jim Morrissette Past Chair, Labor Coalition Cornell University Security Employees Uni Nationwide, Plant Closing Legislation is an idea for which the time is right. From Maine to California, South Carolina to Wisconsin, Philadelphia to Boston, this kind of legislation is providing workers with pro- tection against the trauma of business closings, reductions and relocations. . In 1985, the Tompkins/Cortland Labor Coalition proposed similar legislation for the City of Ithaca. The principles behind the law were soon endorsed by many local organizations and individuals, including Mayor John Gutenberger, the Ithaca Friends Meeting, and the Planning and Development Com- mittee of Common Council. When passed, the law wouldFéqnire bfsinesses in the City to provide workers with 30 to 90 days notice of any impending closings, reductions and reloca- tions. In addition, any financial assistance from the City to new firms would be tied to further protec- tions. Firms would provide severance pay and some continuing health benefits. Workers would also get paid time off to look for new work. Just as trade unions have joined together in the past to fight for laws which have benefitted all of on society — great accomplishments like child labor laws, minimum wages, the 40-hour work week, paid holidays, and affirmative action — so the members of the Labor Coalition have taken the lead in proposing a first step toward responsible planning for the future of Ithaca. At present, the Mayor has appointed an ad hoc committee to study, discuss, and make recommenda- tions on the proposed legislation. Members of the committee are: Ray VanHoutte, Past President of Tompkins County Area Development; Bill Bennet, Past President, Tompkins County Chamber of Com- merce; Charlie French, Building Trades Union; Dick Sullivan, Machinists’ Union; Don Chandler, Precision Filters, Inc.; and Jim Past Chair, Labor Coalition All concerned citizens should contact the Mayor and their representatives on Common Council to urge positive action on Plant Closing Legislation now. Let's not wait for crises as experienced by our neighbors in Groton, Cortland, and Elmira. Let's make sure that business serves the interests and welfare of the people rather than vice versa. “Miss Dugan, will you send someone in here who can distinguish right from wrong?” The Working Press The Working Press is the Publication of the Tompkins - Cortland Labor Coalition. by Jeanne Fudala CSEA For years, the Tompkins County Board of Representatives has missed opportunities to sell the “Old Now the Board, dominated by Republicans, is determined to move the Department of Social Services to the Old Hospital in the face of significant opposition from constituents and evidence that the move would be detrimental to clients. On December 18, 1985, the Board voted to relocate DSS to the Old Hospital (also known as the Biggs Complex). The matter was brought up for recon- sideration when the newly elected Board was seated in January. The new Board tabled the matter until February 18. During that time, the City of Ithaca came forward with a generous proposal to give up City Hall to DSS and relocate the City government. The City was con- cerned with the impact of the proposed move on DSS clients and on downtown businesses. The proposal in- volved the cooperative efforts of Democratic Mayor John Gutenberger and the new Republican County Board Chair, Mary Call. In spite of the City’s offer and statements demonstrating the detrimental impact of such a move on DSS clients, the Board voted 8 to 7 to move DSS. Except for Mary Call, the vote was strictly along party lines. Particularly reprehensible was the vote of Jeff True, the new District 1 Board represen- tative. True acted against the interests of his consti- tuency by voting for the move. Carl H. Feuer Cortland Chapter United University Professions Two days after the vote, a petition drive opposing the DSS move was launched. A total of 4,500 signatures were presented at the Board meeting on March 4th. On March 8, an organization called RESCIND was formed to represent the various groups opposed to the move. The acronym was chosen because this coalition of social services clients, employees and other County residents is asking the Board to “‘re- its decision to move DSS to the Old Hospital. Concern for client accessibility is the primary issue in this effort. Clients within the City who are now able to walk to the DSS offices would have to pay busfare to the Old Hospital; clients coming from other areas of the County would have to make bus connections or travel further by car. For various reasons, many clients have to report to DSS several times a week. Additionally, many clients receive services from other agencies, most of which are located within five blocks of the present DSS location. Clients would thus have to shuttle back and forth between offices; some are likely to fall through the cracks. It would not be surprising if this was one feature of the hidden agenda of some proponents of the move. Additional issues include employee morale, quences to downtown businesses, long range and hid- den costs, and the real costs of all this to the tax base. Our efforts to secure an adequate contract were stymied by the State's Taylor law which forbids strikes by public employees. Nonetheless, at Cortland there was an impressive degree of militancy and solidarity. When we called a general meeting to vote on the for exam- ple, 150 members turned out, voted unanimously to support the action and then picketed our local ad- ministration building. The issues we raised, and will con- tinue to raise, relate to more than our conditions of work. Working people in the State of New York depend on the SUNY system to provide higher education for themselves and their children. That system of public higher education is being sharply eroded by the politicians and budget bureaucrats in Albany. The four-year colleges, such as our campus in Cort- land, have seen sharp cuts in resources, larger classes, declining morale and generally worsening con- ditions. It is likely that this erosion will continue in the future. County Bd. The Salt of the Earth By federal law, two openings must be available to underground workers. Looks like Cargill wants to shut down the workforce too while they rebuild. Cargill has to shut down one shaft to rebuild it. Bob Perkins on strike. Frank Febus. Production Miner A. There's a lot of salt in Tompkins County, and it’s not all on the roads. This salt is part of large underground deposits that the Indians traded, that gave Syracuse the “Salt name, and that runs just about to Detroit, Michigan. There's been a mine at Lansing since the early 1900s, says Bob Perkins, a Production Miner at Cargill. Bob’s been in the mine since 1966. “We were on the 1800 (feet below ground) level when I came here and we've gone back up and under the Harbor. We went down on this new level and expanded about to North Triphammer, along in there. We had to pull out because we couldn't hold the roof; it started crumbling. So we moved in under the lake — right out in the middle of the lake and we just made the turn and we're heading north. Supposed to be going up there two The 140 I.A.M. miners are now working 2200 or 2300 feet below the ground, under Cayuga Lake. In the last year, those 140 men and women mined just about a million tons of salt. “We drill it, undercut it; we got a machine like a big giant chain saw with electric motors, hydraulic,” said Bob. “Then we blast it, dig it out with a front end loader. Put it on a belt line and send it to the surface.” According to Bob, safety condi- tions are good in the mine. come a long, long ways down there compared to what it used to be. They've done a tremendous job down there as far as safety goes, safety conscious.” “I've always said to people at home that it is just as safe down there as Main Street in Groton at 4 o'clock when Smith Corona used to let out. They came tearing through Main Street, trying to be the first one home.”

100 Years Ago What May Day is About By Skye Milliman Painters Local 178 May 1, 1986, marks the 100th anniversary of one of the major struggles waged by our forebears in the labor movement — the eight-hour-day strikes of 1886, centered in Chicago. Workers, long shackled by work days of twelve hours or more for pennies a day, were rallying in great numbers to the cry, “Eight hours for work, eight hours for rest, and eight hours to do what you Men and women whispered it in the workplaces, they talked of it in the taverns and in their homes, till at last they shouted it on the street- comers and from the rooftops. The swelling tide of unrest reached a peak in Chicago that spring, as humanitarian groups, labor unions, and radical agitators alike gathered beneath the banner and stir- red the waters. Meanwhile. the Knights of Labor, a very conser- vative organization which had been the labor power of the past but was in decline. and a fledgling group called the Amalyamated ‘Trades and Labor Assembly, were engaged in a tug of war for the allegiance of American workers. desperate move to gain power und undermine the Knights. Sam Gompers disbanded his group. and at the in- stigation of MeGuire's Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners, issued a call that the eight- hour work day should begin on May Ist, 1886. The reluctant Knights had no choice but to join in the eight-hour fight and try to regain the worker's support, thus engaging their organization ina bitter struggle which ended disastrously. effectively destroying them and leaving the field clear for Sam Gompers and P.J, McGuire, who re-formed their group under the name American Federation of Labor. Saturday, May Ist, dawned bright and clear as workers lined up to march through the streets, sing- ing and waving flags. \llalong the parade route, the rooftops were lined with armed police, Pinkerton dectectives. and militiamen. Thirteen hundred Na- tional Guardsmen waited nervously in the city’s ar- mories. The festive workers strode through the town and on the lakeshore for speeches and pic- nics, then went home, convinced of their inevitable triumph and warmed by comradeship and unity. The strikes beyan, and within a day or two 65,000 to 80,000 workers walked the picket lines. tion sites were foundries were silent, and load- ed ships futilely at their dock lines, while employers, politicians, and police leaders: scurried about, frantically plotting strategy But on May the peace was shattered. The Mc Cormick Harvester Works was partially replacing 1400 workers locked out since mid-February with three hundred strikebreakers, while a few hundred yards away. August Spies was addressing 6.000 lumber-shovers striking for the eight-hour day Shift-change came at McCormick, pickets began to haruss and attack the scabs, angry lumber-shovers came to help, and within fifteen minutes hundreds of policemen arrived and began clubbing and shooting When the smoke cleared, four workers lay dead and many more wounded. “Bight hours for work, eight hours for rest, and eight hours to do what you will.” August Spies issued a call for a mass rally in Haymarket Square the following day, May 4th. Ina light rain, about 3,000 workers gathered to hear Spies. Albert Parsons, Samuel Fielden, and others speak The mayor of Chicago, Carter H. Harrison, was also there to see that order prevailed. As the rain worsened, the bulk of the crowd went home. as did Spies. Parsons, and the unworried mayor, At that point, Inspector John Bonfeld, angered at the mayor's permissiveness, arrived on the scene with nearly two hundred policemen. Somehow, from somewhere, a bomb was thrown into the middle of the police, and those who did not fall began firing hysterically into the fleeing crowd. Seven policemen died, two hundred workers were injured, and an unknown number were killed. In the aftermath of the disastrous Haymarket Massacre, eight “ringleaders” stood trial for con- spiracy and murder. All were convicted, although the actual bomb-thrower was never found. Oscar Neebe, Michael Schwab, and Samuel Fielden were sentenced to prison (and later, at a calmer moment in history. pardoned), and. Louis Lingg committed suicide (at least they called it suicide) itt his cell. On November 11, 18) August Spies, George Engel. Adolph Fischer, and Albert Parsons were hanged, while August Spies’ last words rang in the ears of the spectators and of the world: There will be a time when our silence will be more powerful than the voices you strangle today.” The Haymarket Martyrs were buried and the Knights of Labor disintegrated. The eight-hour movement crushed...but only for a time, and in later years as August Spies’ last words echoed through time, it was revived, and grew, and through more struggle and fice, the cause that the Haymarket Martyrs gave their lives for triumphed. and became the standard for the world. Health Care and Technical Employees Ithaca Health Care and Technical Employees Lodge, Local #1608, LA.M., is the newest Local in town. Final approval was received the last week of march for the new Local. Protect Our Jobs — Buy Union By Edmond M. Ritchie Business Representative Painters Local 178 As we all know, unemployment is one of the most serious problems our country faces today. In spite of an apparently strong economy, people are still find- ing it difficult to find gainful, meaningful employ- ment. What I mean by gainful and meaningful employment is employment that one can hope to port oneself with, and reasonably expect to have the necessities of life and a few luxuries also. The cost of a worn out tire on a car, for example, should not disrupt your financial planning to the point where a person cannot pay the rent or buy food. However, this if often the case. The few jobs that are available today are in the low paid service sector of our economy, such as fast food chains, convenience stores, etc. These jobs are often minimum wage jobs and have no benefits. Why is this the case? It is because of the decline of our higher paying manufacturing industries and the lack of good jobs within those industries. Too many people are competing for too few jobs. Labor is easy and cheap to obtain in these circumstances, and the service sector takes advantage of this. There are no higher paying jobs to compete for. Cargill and the City of Buffalo In 1937, Cargill purchased the Electric grain elevator in Buffalo. Two years later, the company bought the Superior elevator, and in 1964 added the Pool elevator, to give Cargill a 12.8 million bushel total storage capacity in Buf- falo. Then, beginning in 1965, declining grain receipts and other market factors caused a series of temporary shut- downs of these facilities. At this point, it was publicly revealed for the first time that Cargill owed the city and county $896,282 in un- paid back taxes on the three elevators. The company had refused to pay any taxes since 1971, on the ground that the property was overassessed. The Mayor's Task Force on Blight also revealed that Cargill had been stripping the elevators of valuable assets in secret since 1971. Through the Task Force, the public learned that during the period when Cargill refused to pay taxes on the allegedly un- profitable elevators it received over $3 million in grain storage payments from the federal government. 0 Editorial Who Labor Supports For working people, choosing who will govern us in local, State, and National government is a simple extension of the right to participate in making decisions in the workplace over wages, benefits, and working conditions. Our Labor Coalition is a group of Unions, working men and women try- ing to out” for each other. Electing politicians who will “look out” for our interests can be as important as our ef- forts to win fair contracts from Management. If you're a Building Trades Member, you're concerned about prevailing wage legislation; rules that prevent contrac- tors from paying below scale wage rates in order to under-bid a job. If you're a Ithaca Teachers’ Association member you may be worried that the recent political storm over the “sorry state of Education” may be taking a direction that does little for your profession. If you're a government employee you may be restricted from exercising your right to strike by laws like the Taylor Law. If you're a Dining worker at Cornell, you were victimized by a Republican-sponsored amendment that stripped you of your eligibility for unemployment insurance when laid off be- tween semesters. If you're of the Machinists’ Union, unfair foreign competition may leave you with no job. Whatever “type” of worker you are, whatever Union you belong to, you are affected in large and small ways by politics. We are in politics, like it or not. Our Labor Coalition has been pushing hard for some kind of advance notice, or Closing” legislation to give workers fair warning of job loss and some minimal support such as extended health insurance coverage. We have also supported efforts to keep Social Services downtown where it would be best for clients and employees. These issues help show us who our political friends and enemies reall y are. In the Cargill struggle, cooperation from Assemblyman Bar- baro and negligent apathy from our own Sam MacNeil helps remind us of the difference between a politician who will work with us, and one who postures and does nothing. On the basis of a series of conversations at our Labor Coalition meetings, the Labor Coalition has decided that there is substantial support among our member Unions for three candidates this November. Luster For State Assembly Marty Luster has shown us a meaningful sensitivity to labor issues. He was out on the Cargill picket line, he has made clear statements opposing the national trend toward labor bashing, and he is not afraid to speak up for the com- mon person's interests. By contrast, Sam MacNeil has done virtually nothing to distinguish himself, either as an Assemblyman in general, or for working people in particular. For more specifics, see the article in this issue. Morgan For State Senate Matt Morgan has the backing of every area Union in at- tendance at recent Labor Coalition meetings. He has ex- perience in Albany as a lobbyist, and he has reached out to organized labor in his campaign. He has been accessible, always ready to listen, and he has respected position on many issues. He too, has demonstrated real interest in helping the Cargill strike come to a fair conclusion. His oppo- nent has shown little interest in addressing any of labor's concerns. Matt Morgan is our recommendation for State Senate. Cuomo For Governor Finally, we recommend supporting Governor Cuomo for reelection. While he has not always been a good faith bargainer with some public employee organizations, his overall record is one of steady support for Unions. Cuomo’s opponent has done little besides take cheap shots at Cuomo. Also, we wonder where zeal for massive tax cut- ting will leave our much needed education programs and social services. Sentiments in other races were either too divided to take a position or too lukewarm to warrant a recommendation. As trade Unionists we should make the effort to vote for our friends on November 4. In his term as Governor of New York he has done well, winning the support of labor and setting the state on a progressive economic course. He is almost cer- tain to win re-election, and during his next term he may deal with issues in the state with an eye on the needs of a larger constituency. Cuomo was an early supporter of the recently passed tox- ic tort bill (S.9391-A), which changed the statute of limita- tions for actions based on exposure to toxic substances. Under the old law, victims had only a few years from the time of exposure, but now the statute begins to run from the time of discovery of an injury. This list of operations is incomplete, of course. In the miscellaneous category, Cargill trades and transports cof. fee, cotton, wool, petroleum, peanuts, molasses, and vegetable oils. Kates More than 800 rank and file activists, local officers, business agents, union staffers, and other union supporters met in Detroit on Nov. 14-16 to discuss how to “put the movement back in the labor movement.” The conference was organized by Labor Notes, a Detroit-based newsletter published by the Labor Education and Research Project, an inde - educational organization founded in 1978 to “assist and educate union members who are at- tempting to revitalize the American labor movement.” The theme of the meeting, which attracted partici - pants from 10 countries, 32 states, and 70 U.S.- - .based unions, was finding new directions for labor in the current environment of concession-bargaining, plant closings, union-busting, and weakness within the AFL-CIO organizational structure. Goals of the conference were to identify militant strategies that work, develop networks of labor activists, and begin to create an international labor movement committed to solidarity, union democracy, and organizing the unorganized. The panel on New Unionism in the Third World, which opened the conference, included militant union leaders from El Salvador, South Africa, the Philippines, Brazil, and Mexico. Their stories of brutal ‘and repressive treatment under US-backed regimes which do not permit independent union activity were clearly shocking to many trade unionists in the audience. José Rivas, a member of the Social Security Workers Union in El Salvador, said that over 5000 workers of different unions have been killed since 1979, and that all union members share this risk. For example, all the unionized electricians in the country were put in prison for 5 years and then exiled to Holland as political prisoners. Rivas noted that strikers. in his country must take over the work place or they will be shot outside. However, the government normally sends troops into the factories to end strikes, killing or imprisoning strike leaders. When his own union went on strike against a wage freeze imposed in 1980, soldiers broke into a hospital occupied by strikers and Rivas was forced to take sanctuary in the U.S. He told the audience that this year all the unions in El Salvador have united to fight the government, forming the 200,000 member Alliance of Salvadorean Workers Unions. Despite the risk of union activity (“all union members are practically he said people prefer to die by being shot to dying of hunger. Rivas ended his presentation by calling for united action by US and Latin American workers against multinational corporations which operate in their countries. Today, if there is a strike in the US, strikers are replaced or the factory shuts down and re-opens in Latin America. Latin American strikers are handled by the military. Only international union solidarity can begin to change this situation. This year, 262 union leaders have been assassinated. The theme of international solidarity was devel - oped further by Alberto Eulalio, Director of the Metal Workers Union of Brazil. Eulalio described the history of the Central Union, which represents 11 millién workers. In response to military repression, the union formed a political party of the workers (the Workers Party), which is struggling for democratic elections, an end to the wage freeze, a minimum wage and a 40- hour work week, and agrarian reform (3% of the people own 80% of the land). These demands are considered “subversive” by the government and the corporations, which routinely fire any employees dis - covered to belong to the Central Union or the Workers Party. This year, 262 union leaders have been assassinated. Government agencies favor the com - pany and actively help that company in Stealing from the workers their right to a fair wage and safe working conditions. New Organizing Strategies for Labor by C. Kates Most people agree that the labor movement is going through a difficult period. What can we do to turn the tide? The recent national conference on “New Directions for Labor,” sponsored by the Labor Notes newsletter, featured a panel on just this question. It provided much food for thought. Baldemar Velasquez of the Farm Labor Organizing Committee (FLOC) argued that farm workers and small farmers should be allies against large food processing corporations such as Campbell. FLOC advocates 3-party bar - gaining among workers, farmers and the corporations that deal with farmers as inde - pendent contractors. He first tried this with Campbell in 1978, and after 7 years of struggle reached an agreement. Campbell is now contracting crops grown in Mexico, so FLOC plans to go to Mexico to talk with the workers there about solidarity and coordinated union activities. prevented the company from breaking the union by "running the shop backwards." Joe Smith of the UAW (Local 282) described how his 500 employee shop prevented the company from breaking the union by "running the shop backwards.” Although the company had a 30-40% return on-equity, management wanted wage concessions of $3-4/hour, a wage freeze, an end to the COLA, and a new insurance co-payment. The company expected the union to strike, and had already recruited scab replacements. Instead of striking, the local decided to work literally “by the rules,” using no short cuts but following all company procedures. They slowed production by 50%. Workers knew exactly how many days inventory the company had on each item, so they were able to determine the best way to hurt the company by losing part orders or item numbers of. critical parts, or performing complete overhauls rather than making patch repairs on equipment. They also started taking days off at critical periods, and holding mass grievances, bringing 60 em - ployees into an office for some complaint. The company began to lose customers, and inven - tories, which had been high at the outset, were reduced to 3 days. At that point the local went on strike. There was also a presentation by Ray Rogers (Corporate Campaign, Inc.) about ways of attacking a company indirectly through its political and economic power base. Rogers talked about the Hormel campaign, suggesting the defeat of the strike was caused by the UCFW International leadership. An entire workshop devoted to "The Lessons of P-9" echoed this belief. Jim Guyette, suspended president of P- 9, and 20 P-9 members argued that their fight for justice and union democracy was not over. Guyette said without local union militancy and sacrifice the labor movement can- not defend Itself against the unprece- dented and escalating attack by corporate America. Concessions, participa - tion in management “teams,” and business-as- usual unionism will destroy the gains which labor has made through the last 50 years of struggle. A conference highlight was an emotional speech by long-time labor leader Victor Reuther A conference highlight was an emotional speech by long-time labor leader Victor Reuther, who linked the new generation of labor militants with his own generation. He said what he ‘had heard at the conference made him hopeful that others shared his anger at labor leaders who are attacking union democracy and giving away what previous generations fought to achieve. Going Backwards Paul Buhl Wednesday, May 13 was round four of Local 2300's wage reopener talks with Comell University. UAW Local 2300 has got to feel that they're on the right track when the air on Wednesday became thick with Cornell charges of “ridiculous numbers" and scoldings for recent articles mentioning the "S*-word [strike]. The Cornell-UAW Meetings over the past four months were building up to the exchange of proposals and counterproposals, with Comell's proposition of last week amounting to little more than a modification of the current SO grade system. The insulting numbers thrown in, amounting to what is basically a nickel raise, were clearly Part of the bargaining tactic of starting low, but the Proposed raises were really a slap at the UAW. Manager of Employee Relations Pete Tufford had several things to say about Loca! 2300's Proposed six grade, seven step system; Predictably, none of them were good. The main objection that has come up repeatedly is that the UAW proposal is too expensive and too difficult to implement. Tufford refers to the difficulty encountered in implementing a similar system for Operating Engineers. The UAW for its part has managed to do their own research, development and costing on lowly Personal Computers and through Cathy Valentino's calculations. The obvious question raised by Pete Tufford's “logistical nightmare” is what good are supercomputers if they can't be put to a worthwhile human cause such as instituting a fair and sensible Pay system? At the outset of Wednesday's bargaining, Pete Tufford Pronounced the UAW proposal to be “way out of line" and calculated the total cost of the Package to be 4 million dollars in the first year of implementation. This figure as it turns out is based on Cornell's calculating two raises ina year's time, one this July that would bring workers to the minimum of a given grade, and one in January for a year of accrued seniority. Cathy Valentino urged the distraught Cornell negotiators to “rest assured that we only want @ once-a-year increase,” meaning that in July, bargaining unit members will be boosted to the appropriate grade based on calendar year of hire. Any Negotiated increase in future contract bargaining would result in the whole step system moving up, so that seniority progression would mean a step up to a renegotiated higher pay level. Cornell made it clear in their counter Proposa!, cryptically labeled “wages,” that they haven't quit thinking that bargaining unit members have to do a lot more crawling before they can even consider standing. The Comell proposal took no account of employees’ years of service, a source of many existing inequities. Their Proposal consists basically of a slightly upgraded version of their 11 grade SO Pay scale. The proposed wage hike was 10 cents an hour, with the exception of workers at or above the grade “who would receive 50% of the negotiated adjustment in a one-time lump sum payment.” Basically the Cornell proposal amounts to a nickel an hour raise for long service employees. Though Pete Tufford insisted that, union negotiators “look at the concept and not at the numbers,” the Stinginess of their proposal could go unrebutted. Perry Huested spoke of the frustration for all of those Present: “You can't ignore the numbers, this is 2 Slap, it’s falling back to the tactics of ridiculousness of yesterday. When vou see a billion dollars in construction, beautiful buildings, Supercomputers, it just goes to show you Can't judge a book by its cover.” The UAW is going to come back to the bargaining table on May 27 at 2:30, looking to negotiate seriously about a serious issue—fair and decent wages that take into account years of service.
